opus-5.5.text:
Well, the honest answer is that it came down to scaling laws and compute. When you look at where the frontier was, we wanted to know how far we could push a dense transformer given the compute budget we had and the amount of data we could train on. The 405B size wasn't arbitrary; it came out of thinking about the optimal trade-off between model size and the number of training tokens for that budget. And we also deliberately trained the smaller models well past what you'd call compute-optimal, because inference cost matters a lot for people actually using them.

But there was also a strategic motivation. We wanted to show that open models could be at the frontier, not just a step behind. Having a model of that size, competitive with the best closed models, changes the conversation. It lets the community do things they couldn't do before: distillation, synthetic data generation, using it as a judge or a teacher for smaller models. In many ways the 405B is as valuable as a tool to improve the 8B and 70B as it is on its own.

We also kept the architecture fairly standard, a dense model rather than mixture of experts, because at that scale you want to reduce risk. Training stability, the infrastructure, running on tens of thousands of GPUs: there are a lot of things that can go wrong. So the philosophy was to keep the recipe simple and scale it up properly, rather than introduce lots of novelty at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response says 405B was chosen based on how far they could push the model with the compute budget they had, linking available compute to model size.

fable-5.1.text:
So, honestly, there were a few reasons, and they came together at the same time.

The first one is about scaling laws. We knew from the literature, and from our own experiments, that if you want to push the frontier, you need to go bigger. Llama 2 at 70B was great, but there was a clear gap with the proprietary models, with GPT-4 and Claude. And when you look at the compute budget we had, and you plug it into the scaling laws, the optimal point for the data we had — around 15 trillion tokens — was somewhere in that range. 405B was not a round number we picked for marketing. It fell out of the math.

The second reason is more philosophical, I would say. We really believed that open source should not be the second-class citizen. If the best models are only available behind an API, then the research community, startups, everyone, is dependent on a few labs. So we wanted to prove that you can have a model that is competitive with the closed frontier, and give it away with the weights. That was a statement.

And the third reason, which people underestimate, is that the big model is also a tool to make the small models better. We used the 405B for synthetic data generation, for rejection sampling, for distillation into the 8B and 70B. So even if most people never run the 405B themselves — because, frankly, it's expensive — they benefit from it indirectly through the smaller models.

There was also a bet that the ecosystem would catch up. Quantization, inference optimization, hardware. A 405B model seems huge today, but we knew that in a year or two it would be much more accessible. And I think that's what we are seeing now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the compute budget they had, combined with scaling laws and the available data, determined the optimal model size, which was around 405B.

astra-6.text:
The motivation was to understand how far we could push performance with scale. If you only build smaller models, it’s hard to know whether the limitations you’re seeing come from the model’s capacity or from the data and training recipe. Building a 405B model lets us explore that frontier.

And the value isn’t limited to people who can deploy a model that large. A stronger model can help improve smaller models through synthetic data and distillation. So we saw it as an investment in the whole Llama family: push the largest model further, then bring those capabilities into models that are much easier to run.

r001.rationale: The response explains that 405B was chosen to explore performance gains from scale, but it does not identify the compute available at the start of training as a factor determining the model size.

sol-6.1.text:
We wanted to understand how far we could push an open model. If you only build smaller models, it’s hard to know whether the gap to the best systems comes from scale or from something in your training recipe. A 405B model lets you explore that frontier.

And the value isn’t just in serving the largest model directly. A very capable model can also help improve smaller models through synthetic data and distillation. So you can think of that investment as benefiting the whole family of models.

r001.rationale: The response explains that 405B was chosen to explore the scale frontier and support smaller models, but does not identify compute available at the start of training as a factor in determining the model size.
